article.headline: Why Today's S&P 500 Margins Dwarf the Dot-Com Era
article.lede: A chart from BCA Research, circulating widely among macro traders in May 2026, shows S&P 500 net profit margins at their highest level in more than 15 years — roughly 13%, nearly double what prevailed at the peak of the dot-com bubble. Danish macro strategist Andreas Steno made the comparison explicit: this margin surge, he noted, did not happen ahead of the technology bust of 2000. Whether the difference is structural or cyclical is the live debate.
article.body:
A BCA Research chart — shared by Peter Berezin and amplified by Danish macro strategist Andreas Steno — plots **S&P 500 net profit margins** against a decade of history. The metric, calculated as earnings per share divided by sales per share (*EPS/SPS*), reached 13.4% on a blended basis in Q1 2026, the highest level in more than 15 years according to FactSet (FDS) data. Sell-side consensus projects further expansion toward 14.6% by late 2026.

The dot-com contrast is the point. In late 1999, those same margins sat at roughly 7%; at the Nasdaq's peak in early 2000, they barely nudged above 7.4% before collapsing. The late-1990s bull market was driven by *price-to-sales* multiples — a valuation method indifferent to profitability — applied liberally to companies, many running deeply negative margins, with no near-term path to profit. Steno's observation is precise: whatever risks the current rally carries, it is sitting on a different earnings foundation than the bubble that burst in 2000.

Structural changes in the index explain much of the gap. Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Nvidia (NVDA), Alphabet (GOOGL), and Meta Platforms (META) now represent roughly 30% of the index by weight, each carrying net margins between 20% and 50%. In 2000, the heaviest index weights included telecoms and hardware companies with thinner margins, while the most celebrated internet names were largely pre-revenue. Layered on top: AI-driven *operating leverage* — the dynamic by which fixed-cost infrastructure produces rising margins as revenue scales — slowing wage inflation, and the 2025 tax legislation.

The metric itself warrants scrutiny. EPS/SPS captures net income after interest and taxes, not operational efficiency alone; the 2025 tax cuts mechanically improved net margins without a corresponding change in business fundamentals. FactSet's tracking of this series begins only in 2009, so the dot-com comparison relies on third-party datasets with different methodologies. Consensus estimates of 14.6% for late 2026 carry the upward bias typical of sell-side forecasting. And *capex* cycles — heavy investment spending on chips and data centres that precedes, and may eventually compress, returns — have not been fully priced into those projections.

The irony is that Berezin himself ranks among the more cautious institutional strategists on the current cycle. BCA Research has warned that AI capital expenditure may peak within 12 months, drawing comparisons to the telecom overbuilding that preceded the dot-com crash. Sharing a chart of record margins can be read as diagnosis rather than celebration — record margins are as plausibly a ceiling as a foundation. Whether today's earnings power is secular or cyclical will determine how this data point ages.

concepts.definition: A measure of aggregate corporate profitability calculated by dividing earnings per share by sales per share — equivalent to net profit margin at the index level. It captures the bottom line after all costs including interest and taxes. Unlike operating margin, it is sensitive to tax law changes and financing costs, which can shift the figure without any change in underlying business performance.

A stock valuation ratio comparing a company's share price to its annual revenue per share. Unlike price-to-earnings, it can be applied to unprofitable companies, making it a favoured metric during the dot-com era when many celebrated names had no earnings to value. A high multiple implies investors expect margins to improve substantially in the future.

The degree to which a company's cost structure allows revenue growth to produce disproportionately larger profit growth. A firm with high fixed costs and low marginal costs — cloud software, semiconductor design — exhibits strong operating leverage: once infrastructure is built, each additional dollar of revenue contributes more to the bottom line.

Spending on long-lived physical or intangible assets — servers, data centres, chip fabrication lines — expected to generate returns over several years. In the current AI cycle, hyperscalers are committing tens of billions annually; whether those investments will yield sufficient returns is one of the central macro debates of 2025-2026.

The well-documented tendency for equity analysts at investment banks to publish earnings and margin forecasts that are systematically too high, particularly for periods more than two quarters out. The bias reflects both commercial incentives and the difficulty of accounting for macro shocks not yet visible in the data.

ticker_fds.name: FactSet Research Systems Inc.
ticker_fds.blurb: FactSet Research Systems Inc. is a financial digital platform and enterprise solutions provider serving the investment community. The company delivers data, analytical applications, workstations, portfolio analytics, and enterprise data solutions, along with managed services supporting data, performance, risk, and reporting workflows. It offers subscription-based financial data and market intelligence covering securities, companies, industries, and individuals, enabling buy-side and sell-side professionals to research investments and manage portfolios. With roughly 12,800 employees and a trailing-twelve-month revenue of approximately $2.40 billion, FactSet competes directly with Bloomberg and Refinitiv (LSEG) in the financial data terminal and analytics market.
ticker_fds.recent: As of mid-May 2026, FDS shares trade near $199.86 — close to their 52-week low of $185.00 and down sharply from a 52-week high of $474.79, reflecting a market-cap contraction of roughly 55.6% over the past year. The analyst consensus stands at Hold with an average price target of $284.80, implying significant upside from current levels but signaling caution. The company has a quarterly earnings report scheduled for June 22, 2026, and an ex-dividend date of May 29, 2026 for its $4.40 annual dividend.

ticker_aapl.name: Apple Inc.
ticker_aapl.blurb: Apple designs and markets consumer electronics (iPhone, Mac, iPad, Apple Watch), software, and digital services. The iPhone remains the dominant revenue driver, but the Services segment — comprising the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud, Apple Pay, and licensing — has grown into a high-margin business that Wall Street values separately. Apple commands one of the highest brand loyalty rates in consumer technology and operates a tightly integrated hardware-software ecosystem.
ticker_aapl.recent: Apple reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $400 billion. The company has faced headwinds from slowing iPhone upgrade cycles in mature markets and regulatory pressure on App Store commissions in both the US and EU. Apple Intelligence, its generative AI suite, launched in late 2024 but has not yet materially re-accelerated upgrade cycles. Paul Pelosi sold 45,000 shares of AAPL according to the January 2026 PTR disclosure — the largest single sale in the filing by share count.

ticker_msft.name: Microsoft Corporation
ticker_msft.description: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.blurb: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.recent: As of early May 2026, MSFT trades near $413 — down approximately 25.6% from its July 31, 2025 all-time high of $555.45 and -15.7% YTD — after touching a March 28 correction low of $356.07. The drawdown carried the stock briefly below its 200-week moving average for the first time in roughly 13 years (prior touches: 2009, 2018, 2020, 2022). Revenue grew 18% YoY with Azure +40%, while annualized AI revenue reached approximately $37 billion; calendar-2026 capex is projected near $190 billion and free cash flow contracted -22% YoY. Forward P/E is approximately 24.4.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_googl.name: Alphabet Inc. (Class A)
ticker_googl.blurb: Alphabet is the parent company of Google, the world's dominant search engine, as well as YouTube, the Google Cloud Platform, and a portfolio of moonshot bets (Waymo, DeepMind, Verily). Search advertising accounts for the majority of revenue, but the cloud division has grown into a multi-billion-dollar profit centre. Alphabet is also a leading player in generative AI, having developed the Gemini family of large language models and integrated them across its product suite.
ticker_googl.recent: Alphabet reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $370 billion, with Google Cloud crossing $50 billion annually. The company has faced antitrust scrutiny in both the US and EU, with a US federal court ruling in 2024 that Google holds an illegal monopoly in general search. Despite regulatory headwinds, the stock has benefited from AI-driven search enhancements and strong cloud growth. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026) gaining approximately 75% over the period.

sources.title: Nancy Pelosi's 2026 Stock Moves — Motley Fool

ticker_meta.name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
ticker_meta.blurb: Meta Platforms, headquartered in Menlo Park, California, operates Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — collectively the largest social-media ecosystem in the world by monthly active users. The company generates the vast majority of its revenue through digital advertising, using detailed behavioural data to target ads across its platforms. After a painful 2022 in which shares fell roughly 65% amid a revenue slowdown and ballooning metaverse losses, Meta executed a dramatic turnaround by cutting costs, boosting margins, and rapidly integrating AI-driven ad ranking tools (Advantage+) that demonstrably improved advertiser returns. CEO Mark Zuckerberg declared 2023 a 'Year of Efficiency' and the company followed through. By late 2025 Meta was simultaneously the most profitable it had ever been and the most aggressive in AI infrastructure spending, committing up to $65 billion in capex for 2025 and raising that figure to as much as $145 billion for 2026.
ticker_meta.recent: Meta reached an all-time high near $796 per share in September 2025. The stock declined approximately 24–28% from that peak through April 2026, with the primary investor concern being the scale of the 2026 capital-expenditure commitment — up to $145 billion — and uncertainty about whether AI-driven revenue would materialise at the pace required to justify it. Quarterly earnings remained strong through the period, but multiple compression drove share-price weakness.

poster_andreassteno.blurb: Andreas Steno Larsen is a Danish macro strategist and founder of Andreas Steno Research, an independent macro research firm. He previously served as Chief FX & Fixed Income Strategist at Nordea Markets, one of Scandinavia's largest banks. On X he posts global macro analysis with a focus on central bank policy, global liquidity cycles, inflation, and the macro case for crypto assets. He has built a substantial following — likely in the 200–300k range — among macro traders, portfolio managers, and finance-adjacent audiences.
poster_andreassteno.credibility_note: Well-regarded in macro trading circles for liquidity-framework calls and early crypto-macro crossover work. No major public corrections or controversies known, though like most macro forecasters his directional calls carry inherent uncertainty. Runs a paid research service, which is worth noting when evaluating the framing of his public posts.
